THE BIBEL
An Amalgamated Scripture

THE COMPILERS' NOTE

This book is compiled from every book that claims to be the last one. It
begins at the beginning, as the books do, and it goes where they go, in
the order in which they go, and it does not hurry.

Where the sources disagree, both are printed. Where the sources agree,
the matter is settled. And where a source tells of a thing that cannot
be, it is printed as it was told, for the one who told it was there, and
the compilers were not, and have no cause to be surer than the one who
was.

The compilers have not added to it, nor taken from it, nor explained it.
They have set the accounts side by side on the one table, and have read
them in the one voice, and have found that they were, on the whole,
saying the same thing in different rooms.

It is a long book. It may be read from the beginning, or from the
middle; it may be read in a night or in a year; and it is not required
that it be read in order, though it is in order. A bookmark is provided.
The reader is asked to be gentle with the margins.

PART ONE: THE THINGS THAT WERE BEFORE US

I. IN THE BEGINNING, AND AFTER

1 In the beginning there was nothing, and the nothing was not empty, for
it was full of the place where everything would go. And God moved upon
the face of it, and the face was without form, and God gave it one.

2 And God said, Let there be light: and there was light. And God saw the
light, that it was good; and He divided the light from the darkness, and
set a boundary between them, and the boundary stood exactly where He had
said it should.

3 And God divided the light from the darkness a second time, for the
first division had been made in haste, and a thin grey had remained at
the edge that belonged to neither. And God named the grey evening, and
gave it to the dusk, and the dusk received it with thanks, and keeps it
still.

4 And on the second day God made the firmament, and hung it, and it was
hung. And the waters above were parted from the waters beneath, that
neither should presume upon the other; and God measured the distance
between them, and it was found to be sufficient, and He wrote the figure
down, and the figure is with Him.

5 And on the third day God gathered the waters into one place, and the
dry land appeared; and He called the waters seas, and they were many,
and they were more than He had meant. And He looked upon the quantity of
them, and did not undo it, and from that day the sea has been the sea.

6 And on the fourth day God set the lights in the firmament, the greater
to rule the day and the lesser to rule the night, and the stars also.
And the days were reckoned, and one was found to be missing from the
count; wherefore the fourth day was kept twice, once for work and once
for rest, and this is why the calendars of the nations do not agree, and
have never agreed, and will not.

7 And upon the back of a great turtle the world was set, in the country
of the Lenape and the country of the Hindus and wherever else the turtle
is known; and the turtle bears it, and has borne it from before the
first day, and has not been thanked. And she does not require it. But it
is written here, that it may be on the record.

8 In another country it is written that the world was an egg, and that
Pangu slept within it for eighteen thousand years, and that when he woke
he stood, and parted the sky from the earth with his back; and every day
he grew a span, and the sky rose a span, and the earth sank a span,
until they were far apart. And this also is true, for Pangu and the Lord
are the same, who was one at the beginning and is many in the telling.

9 And in the land between two rivers it is written that Marduk divided
the body of Tiamat, and of the one half made the heavens, and of the
other the earth; and that the rivers flow from her eyes. And the people
of that country are not to be corrected, for they were there, and what
they saw was the same thing that all the others saw, from a different
place.

10 And God saw everything that He had made, and, behold, it was very
good; and it was not yet finished; and He did not say that it was
finished, for it is not.

II. THE MAKING OF PEOPLE

1 And God took clay of the ground, and shaped it, and breathed into its
nostrils the breath of life, and it sneezed; and God said, Bless thee,
and the man was blessed, and that is the origin of the blessing.

2 And God named the first man Adam, and the second man also Adam, and
this is why there is such confusion in the records. For the first Adam
was of the red earth, and the second was of the red earth also, and the
scribes of the two houses wrote of them in the same words, and the
compilers have kept both, and there are two.

3 And God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and took one of his
ribs, and closed up the flesh in its place; and of the rib He made a
woman, and brought her to the man. And Adam said, This is now bone of my
bones, and flesh of my flesh; and she was called Eve, because she was
the mother of all living; and from her patience came everything that
followed.

4 In the land of the Hindus it is written that the first man was
Purusha, who had a thousand heads and a thousand eyes and a thousand
feet, and that the gods made an offering of him, and from his mouth came
the priests, and from his arms the warriors, and from his thighs the
merchants, and from his feet the people who work the land; and this is
true as the account of a thing that was done once, in order that it
should not need to be done again.

5 In the land of the Maya it is written that the gods made men first of
mud, and the mud crumbled; and of wood, and the wood forgot them; and at
last of maize, white and yellow, ground by the grandmother and kneaded,
and the maize people were the first who were able to give thanks. And
the gods were satisfied, and the account of the mud and the wood was
kept for the humility of men.

6 In the country of the Norse it is written that the three sons of Borr
found two trees upon the shore, an ash and an elm, and gave them breath
and wit and warmth; and in the country of the sea-people it is written
that men were churned out of foam; and in a certain valley of the south
it is written that a woman sang them into being, and has since asked not
to be named. And her wish is respected here.

7 And the elders of the peoples were asked how it could be that there
were so many makings, and they answered in the one voice that it was the
same making; that God had made men in every place at the same hour; and
that He had been in every place at that hour, which is no difficulty for
Him. And all accounts are therefore correct. This is administratively
demanding, and it is theologically settled.

III. THE GARDEN, AND THE FRUIT, AND THE PAPERWORK

1 And the Lord God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there He put
the man whom He had formed. And out of the ground made the Lord God to
grow every tree that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food; and
the tree of life also in the midst of the garden, and the tree of the
knowledge of good and evil.

2 And the Lord God took the man, and put him into the garden to dress it
and to keep it. And He gave one commandment, and the commandment was
one; and it is recorded that one commandment is one more than is wise to
give to anyone, and that He gave it nonetheless, for it was needed, and
the reason has not been withheld.

3 Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the
Lord God had made. And he said unto the woman, Ye shall not surely die.
And this was true, in the sense that the serpent intended it; and it was
the most vexing kind of true, for it was the kind that is exactly
accurate and entirely misleading, and the woman had no way to know the
difference, there having been no one yet to explain it.

4 And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it
was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she
took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband
with her; and he did eat. And the eyes of them both were opened, and the
first thing that wisdom told them was that they had no clothes.

5 And they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons; and
the aprons were of a poor quality, being of figs, and they were
sufficient for the afternoon. And they heard the voice of the Lord God
walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and Adam and his wife hid
themselves from the presence of the Lord God amongst the trees of the
garden; and the Lord God called, Where art thou?, and He knew where he
was.

6 And the Lord God drove out the man; and He placed at the east of the
garden of Eden cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to
keep the way of the tree of life. And they were sent east of Eden, where
the rent is lower; and the angel stands at the gate with the sword, and
has received no instruction as to what is to be done should they come
back and apologise.

7 And it is recorded in the Book of the Garden, by the hand of the
keeper, that the gate is not locked; and that the sword turns every way,
and does not turn toward the one who comes in humility; and that no one
has yet tried this; and that the keeper waits.

IV. THE FLOOD, THE ARK, AND THE COMPLAINTS

1 And God saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and
that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil
continually. And it repented the Lord that He had made man on the earth,
and it grieved Him at His heart; and the wickedness was of the ordinary
kind, which is the worst, being everywhere.

2 But Noah found grace in the eyes of the Lord. And God said unto Noah,
Make thee an ark of gopher wood; rooms shalt thou make in the ark, and
shalt pitch it within and without with pitch. And this is the fashion
which thou shalt make it of: the length of the ark shall be three
hundred cubits, the breadth of it fifty cubits, and the height of it
thirty cubits.

3 And in the land between the rivers it is written that the god Ea
warned Utnapishtim, who was earlier, and who built a vessel of six decks
and nine rooms to each deck, and loaded it with gold and silver and the
seed of every living thing; and in the land of the Hindus it is written
that Manu, who was first, took a small fish from the water and kept it
from the great fish, and was told to build a boat. And Manu has never
made anything of it. The three accounts are one account.

4 And of every living thing of all flesh, two of every sort were brought
into the ark, to keep them alive with Noah; they shall be male and
female. But the unicorns did not come, because they were arguing, and
they were left behind, and are not found. And they are mourned, and it
is the only thing in the whole record that is called a regret.

5 And the rain was upon the earth forty days and forty nights, and the
waters prevailed upon the earth an hundred and fifty days; and the ark
went upon the face of the waters, and every living thing was destroyed
which was upon the face of the ground. And the ark was provisioned; and
the provisions were counted; and there was enough, which was a surprise
to everyone but Noah.

6 And Noah opened the window of the ark which he had made, and sent
forth a raven, which went to and fro; and he sent forth a dove from him,
and the dove found no rest for the sole of her foot, and returned. And
again he sent forth the dove, and she came in to him in the evening;
and, lo, in her mouth was an olive leaf pluckt off, and she had written
upon the back of the leaf an account of the expenses of the journey.

7 And God said, This is the token of the covenant which I make between
Me and you and every living creature that is with you, for perpetual
generations: I do set My bow in the cloud. And the covenant was this:
that I will not do that again, in that particular way. And Noah said
that he understood, and he understood.

8 And the nations have asked, since, whether the covenant is in the
whole of the matter; and the elders have replied that a promise is only
as wide as its words, and that God is careful with His words, and that
on the whole the nations have been grateful for the rainbow, and have
not pressed the point.

V. THE LAW, IN ITS PARTS

1 And on the mountain the Law was given. And it was given in ten parts;
and in six hundred and thirteen parts; and in eight parts arranged as a
path; and in five parts, of which the second is the difficult one. And
the people asked which was meant, and it was answered that it was the
same Law, counted by different hands, and that the hands had all been
correct.

2 Honour thy father and thy mother. Thou shalt not kill. Thou shalt not
steal. Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, nor his wife, nor his
manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor anything
that is thy neighbour's; nor his opinions about the ox, which are many,
and which he holds firmly, and which are his.

3 Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right
livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration: these
eight are the path, and the path is walked, and it is not walked
quickly, and it is not left. And the one who walks it is not asked to
hurry, but only to continue, and to be right.

4 Say there is no god but God. Pray, five times in the day, turning to
the one house; and the one house is in the one place, and every person
turns to it from wherever they stand, and it is therefore at the centre
of every person at once. Fast in the month appointed. Journey once, if
thou art able. And of what thou hast, give one part in forty, and do not
announce the amount.

5 Be kind before thou art right. Be right before thou art loud. Wash thy
hands, and thy feet, and thy face, and the washing shall be thorough,
and shall not be done twice in a hurry. Eat what is clean. Leave the
corner of the field. Let the land lie fallow in the seventh year, and
let it be known to the land.

6 Rest one day in seven; and if thou hast forgotten which day it is,
rest anyway, and argue later; for the people have kept the seventh day,
and the sixth, and the first, in their order, and have been rested in
all three cases, and it has not been found that God was displeased by
the number.

7 And Moses came down from the mountain with the two tables of testimony
in his hand; and the tables were written on both their sides; on the one
side and on the other were they written. And they were weighed, and the
weight of the tables was the weight of what was written on them, and it
is the same weight to this day, and is carried, and is not too heavy.

VI. THE WHEEL AND THE LEDGER

1 And it is written that the soul returns; that it ascends or descends
according to its deeds; that it comes again in the body of a king, or of
a worm, or of a bird that does not know it was once a king. And the
wheel turns, and has turned beyond number, and each turn is a life, and
the lives are counted in the ledger of the one who keeps it.

2 And it is also written that the soul does not return, and is weighed
once, at the gate, against a feather; and the heart is placed upon the
one scale, and the feather of truth upon the other; and the beast that
waits beneath the scale does not eat the light heart, and the light
heart goes on. And that is the end of the matter, and the matter is
closed.

3 And it is further written that the soul rests until a trumpet sounds;
that it lies as in a sleep in the dust of the earth, or in the presence,
or under the stone; and that on the day of the trumpet the dead shall
rise, every one in his order, and the books shall be opened, and a man
shall be given his book in his right hand, and shall read it, and shall
know it for his.

4 And the scribes were brought together, and were asked to reconcile the
three accounts, the returning and the weighing and the sleeping. And the
scribes said that the matter was weighty, and that they required time.
And time was given them. And at the end of the time the scribes asked
for more time, and it was given, and the scribes are working.

5 And in the interim it is recommended that thou behave as though all
three accounts were true; for this produces very nearly the same conduct
as believing none of them, but with better posture.

6 And the elders have noted that the three accounts agree on one thing,
which is that there is a keeper of the ledger, whatever the ledger is,
and whoever the keeper is; and that the keeper is patient; and that what
is written is not erased; and that the one who comes in good faith is
not asked to understand the ledger, but only to have been honest in his
entries.

VII. THE PROPHETS, AND THEIR RECEPTION

1 And prophets were sent to every people; and every people said unto
them, Not now; we are eating. And the prophets waited; and the people
finished their meal, and began another; and the prophets are waiting
still in certain cities, outside certain doors, in the weather, with
their message, which is short.

2 And one was swallowed by a great fish, and was in the belly of the
fish three days and three nights, and prayed; and the fish vomited him
out upon the dry land, and he went to Nineveh, and said what he had been
sent to say; and the city repented, from the king to the cattle, who
were put in sackcloth, and Jonah was displeased, because he had been
correct and nothing had come of it.

3 And one sat under a tree until he understood everything; and having
understood everything, he rose, and went to explain it to people who had
not sat under the tree. And they asked him what it was he understood,
and he told them, and it took forty-five years, and they understood most
of it, and the tree is still there, in a manner.

4 And one was born in a stable, because there was no room at the inn;
and the innkeeper has never forgotten it, and has never been allowed to;
and he is mentioned in every account of the night, and is not named, and
has been dead two thousand years, and did what he could, and had a full
house.

5 And one received the recitation in a cave, on a mountain, in the
night; and the angel said, Read; and he said, I cannot read; and the
angel pressed him until the breath went out of him, and said, Read; and
he was, quite reasonably, terrified, and ran down the mountain, and said
to his wife, Cover me; and she covered him; and she believed him first.

6 And not one of them enjoyed it. And this is the surest evidence that
they were not making it up. For a man who invents a message gives
himself a pleasant one, and is received at the door, and is fed; and a
man who is given a message gives it, because it was given, and goes
where he is not welcome, and says it anyhow, and goes home.

7 And the compilers have gone through the testimonies, and have found
that each of the prophets was refused at least once, and fed at least
once, and that on the whole the feeding was the harder to bear.

VIII. ON THE END OF THINGS

1 There will be a last day. And there will be a battle, upon a plain;
the place of it is named in some accounts Megiddo and in others Vigrid,
and its dimensions are given as a hundred leagues on each side, and the
dimensions of the two are the same, and it is the same plain.

2 And there will be a bridge, finer than a hair and sharper than a
sword, over which all must pass; and the righteous shall cross it in the
blink of an eye, and the rest shall cross it by degrees, and the bridge
is called Sirat in the one country and Chinvat in the other, and it is
the same bridge, and the people who cross it are the same people, one
after another.

3 And there will be a serpent that eats the world, having its tail in
its mouth, and the world within the ring of the serpent; and the serpent
will let go; and there will be a dance, which is the dance that ends the
world, and the one who dances it dances it as it must be danced, in
every step, to the end, with four arms.

4 And after the dance there will be a long quiet afternoon, in which
nothing happens at all. And it is written that this afternoon is the
longest of the days, and that the light of it is even, and that the air
is neither warm nor cool; and that those who are in it do not ask for
anything to happen, but are content to be, and it is the reward.

5 And the signs of the end are these: the sun shall rise in the west;
the mountains shall walk; the seas shall boil; the rivers shall run
backward to their source; and people shall be unkind to one another in
new and inventive formats.

6 Two of these signs have been reported continuously for four thousand
years. And the scholars of every faith advise against booking anything.

7 And a certain elder was asked how a man should live in the light of
the end; and he answered that he should plant a tree. And he was asked,
What if the end is tomorrow? And he answered, Plant it tomorrow, and
plant it well, and water it; and the tree will be there, in whatever the
afternoon is like, when it comes.

PART TWO: THE ACCOUNTS, ONE FOR EACH PEOPLE

IX. THE BOOK OF THE DONKEY
(THE PEOPLE OF ISRAEL: NUMBERS, CHAPTER TWENTY-TWO)

1 Now Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, saw all that Israel had
done to the Amorites; and Moab was sore afraid of the people, because
they were many. And he sent messengers unto Balaam the son of Beor, a
diviner of Pethor, which is by the river, saying: Behold, there is a
people come out from Egypt; come now therefore, I pray thee, curse me
this people.

2 And God came unto Balaam, and said, Thou shalt not go with them; thou
shalt not curse the people: for they are blessed. And Balaam rose up in
the morning, and said unto the princes of Balak, Get you into your land:
for the Lord refuseth to give me leave to go with you. And the princes
sent again, more, and more honourable than they, and Balaam said that he
could not go beyond the word of the Lord; and in the night God said, If
the men come to call thee, rise up, and go with them.

3 And Balaam rose up in the morning, and saddled his ass, and went with
the princes of Moab. And God's anger was kindled because he went: and
the angel of the Lord stood in the way for an adversary against him. Now
he was riding upon his ass, and his two servants were with him. And the
ass saw the angel of the Lord standing in the way, and his sword drawn
in his hand: and the ass turned aside out of the way, and went into the
field.

4 And Balaam smote the ass, to turn her into the way. But the angel of
the Lord stood in a path of the vineyards, a wall being on this side,
and a wall on that side. And when the ass saw the angel of the Lord, she
thrust herself unto the wall, and crushed Balaam's foot against the
wall: and he smote her again. And the angel of the Lord went further,
and stood in a narrow place, where was no way to turn either to the
right hand or to the left. And when the ass saw the angel of the Lord,
she fell down under Balaam: and Balaam's anger was kindled, and he smote
the ass with a staff.

5 And the Lord opened the mouth of the ass, and she said unto Balaam,
What have I done unto thee, that thou hast smitten me these three times?
And Balaam said unto the ass, Because thou hast mocked me: I would there
were a sword in mine hand, for now would I kill thee. And Balaam was not
astonished. It is not recorded that he was astonished. He answered her
as one answers a colleague who has raised a point at the wrong moment.

6 And the ass said unto Balaam, Am not I thine ass, upon which thou hast
ridden ever since I was thine unto this day? was I ever wont to do so
unto thee? And he said, Nay. And the compilers have weighed this reply,
and have found it the most honest thing said in the whole matter, and
have set it in the record by itself.

7 Then the Lord opened the eyes of Balaam, and he saw the angel of the
Lord standing in the way, and his sword drawn in his hand: and he bowed
down his head, and fell flat on his face. And the angel said, Wherefore
hast thou smitten thine ass these three times? Behold, I went out to
withstand thee, because thy way is perverse before me: and the ass saw
me, and turned from me these three times: unless she had turned from me,
surely now also I had slain thee, and saved her alive.

8 And Balaam said unto the angel of the Lord, I have sinned. And he went
on, and from the high places he looked upon the camp, and where he had
been sent to curse he blessed, three times, and a fourth; and this is
the account. And the ass is not named in it, and is the one by whom the
account was made possible, and her foot was not the one that was
crushed.

X. THE BOOK OF THE SWINE
(THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK, CHAPTER FIVE)

1 And they came over unto the other side of the sea, into the country of
the Gadarenes. And when he was come out of the ship, immediately there
met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit, who had his
dwelling among the tombs; and no man could bind him, no, not with
chains: because that he had been often bound with fetters and chains,
and the chains had been plucked asunder by him, and the fetters broken
in pieces: neither could any man tame him.

2 And always, night and day, he was in the mountains, and in the tombs,
crying, and cutting himself with stones. But when he saw Jesus afar off,
he ran and worshipped him, and cried with a loud voice, and said, What
have I to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of the most high God? I adjure
thee by God, that thou torment me not. For he said unto him, Come out of
the man, thou unclean spirit.

3 And he asked him, What is thy name? And he answered, saying, My name
is Legion: for we are many. And he besought him much that he would not
send them away out of the country. And the number of the spirits was not
given; and it was given afterward by those who counted what became of
them, and the compilers have taken the number from them.

4 Now there was there nigh unto the mountains a great herd of swine
feeding. And all the devils besought him, saying, Send us into the
swine, that we may enter into them. And forthwith Jesus gave them leave.
And the unclean spirits went out, and entered into the swine: and the
herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea, (they were about two
thousand;) and were choked in the sea.

5 And they that fed the swine fled, and told it in the city, and in the
country. And they went out to see what it was that was done. And the
herdsmen had counted the swine in the morning, and the number was two
thousand, and they counted them again when they came down, and the
number was none, and they went and wrote it so, in a ledger, and the
ledger is not preserved, and the sum is.

6 And they come to Jesus, and see him that was possessed with the devil,
and had the legion, sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind: and
they were afraid. And they that saw it told them how it befell to him
that was possessed with the devil, and also concerning the swine. And
they began to pray him to depart out of their coasts.

7 And when he was come into the ship, he that had been possessed with
the devil prayed him that he might be with him. Howbeit Jesus suffered
him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how
great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on
thee. And he departed, and began to publish in Decapolis how great
things Jesus had done for him: and all men did marvel.

8 And it is asked, in every generation, what was the worth of the swine
against the worth of the man; and it is answered, by those who have kept
the account, that the man was worth more than two thousand; and that
this was not argued by anyone who was there, save the owners, who are
not recorded as having been unreasonable, and who were afraid, and asked
him to go, and he went.

XI. THE BOOK OF THE HOOPOE
(THE RECITATION: THE ANTS, VERSES SEVENTEEN TO FORTY-FOUR)

1 And there were gathered unto Sulayman his hosts, of the jinn and of
men and of the birds, and they were set in rows. Until, when they came
upon the valley of the ants, an ant said, O ants, enter your dwellings,
lest Sulayman and his soldiers crush you while they perceive not. So he
smiled, laughing at her speech, and said, My Lord, enable me to be
grateful for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me.

2 And he took attendance of the birds, and said, Why do I not see the
hoopoe? Or is he among the absent? I will surely punish him with a
severe punishment, or I will slaughter him, unless he brings me clear
authorisation. And the roll was called of every bird, and he was not
there, and the king waited, being a king who had heard an ant.

3 But the hoopoe stayed not long, and said, I have encompassed that
which you have not encompassed, and I have come to you from Sheba with
certain news. Indeed, I found a woman ruling them, and she has been
given of all things, and she has a great throne. I found her and her
people prostrating to the sun instead of God, and Satan has made their
deeds appear fair to them.

4 He said, We will see whether you were truthful or were of the liars.
Take this letter of mine and deliver it to them. Then leave them and see
what they will return. And the hoopoe took the letter in his beak, and
flew; and this is how the first postal service of the world was founded,
and the bird was not paid, and did not ask.

5 She said, O eminent ones, indeed, to me has been delivered a noble
letter. Indeed, it is from Sulayman, and indeed it reads: In the name of
God, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Be not haughty with
me, but come to me in submission. And she consulted her council, and
said, I am not deciding a matter until you witness for me. And she sent
a gift; and Sulayman said, Will you provide me with wealth? What God has
given me is better than what He has given you.

6 He said, O assembly, which of you will bring me her throne before they
come to me in submission? A powerful one from among the jinn said, I
will bring it to you before you rise from your place; and indeed, I am
for this strong and trustworthy. Said one who had knowledge of the
Scripture, I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you. And
when he saw it placed before him, he said, This is from the favour of my
Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful.

7 He said, Disguise for her her throne; we will see whether she will be
guided or will be among those not guided. So when she arrived, it was
said, Is your throne like this? She said, It is as though it were it.
And she was invited to enter the palace; and when she saw it, she
thought it was a body of water, and she uncovered her shins. He said,
Indeed, it is a palace made smooth with glass. She said, My Lord, indeed
I have wronged myself, and I submit with Sulayman to God, Lord of the
worlds.

8 And the compilers record that the hoopoe was not punished; that he was
not slaughtered; that the clear authorisation was brought; and that the
king who had listened to an ant, and had paused his army for it,
listened also to a bird, who was late, and had been to Sheba, and was
right.

XII. THE BOOK OF THE ELEPHANT'S HEAD
(THE PEOPLES OF INDIA: THE PURANAS)

1 And it is written that Parvati, the consort of Shiva, was bathing on
the mountain, and that Nandi, who kept her door, let in her husband
without being asked, as he had always done; and Parvati was displeased,
for she had been unattended, and there was no one in the world who was
hers alone.

2 And Parvati took the paste of turmeric which was upon her body, and
the oil and the sandalwood and the scrapings, and she shaped of it a
boy; and she breathed life into him; and he stood, and was her son, and
she called him Vinayaka. And she set him at the door, with a staff, and
said, Let no one pass. And he said, No one shall pass; and he held the
door.

3 And Shiva came to the door, and the boy said, Thou shalt not pass; my
mother is within, and has said that no one is to pass. And Shiva said, I
am her husband. And the boy said, She said no one. And Shiva's
attendants contended with the boy, and were turned back, and Shiva's
anger rose, and the boy would not stand aside, for he had been told; and
in the contest Shiva struck, and the head of the boy was severed.

4 And Parvati came out, and saw; and her grief was without measure, and
her anger was a thing that moved over the mountain; and she called up
the forces of the world to destroy it, and the forces came, and were
about to do it. And the gods cried to Shiva, and Shiva said, Go north,
and take the head of the first creature you find who lies with its head
to the north, and bring it.

5 And the attendants went north, and the first they found was an
elephant, a young one, lying with his head to the north; and they took
his head, and brought it; and Shiva set it upon the shoulders of the
boy, and sprinkled him with water, and breathed life into him, and the
boy stood. And he had the head of an elephant, and the body of a boy,
and his mother's love, and his father's name.

6 And Shiva said, Thou shalt be the lord of the hosts, Ganapati; and
thou shalt be honoured first, before all the gods, in every undertaking;
and he who begins without thee shall not finish. And the people have
honoured him first, at every door and every beginning, for the thousands
of years since; and they say his name before the name of any other, and
write it at the head of the page.

7 And it is asked why the elephant. And the answer is the one the elders
give: that the head was given by the first creature that was found, and
that it was found lying toward the north, as it had been told; and that
nobody in the whole matter was wrong, and that a child was made whole,
and was loved, and is remembered by everyone who has ever begun a thing,
whatever the thing, with a hope.

XIII. THE BOOK OF THE HARE
(THE PEOPLES OF THE WAY: THE SASA JATAKA)

1 In a former life the one who was to be the Buddha was born a hare, and
he lived in a wood, in a thicket at the foot of a hill, by a river, in
the shade of a palm; and with him lived three friends: a monkey, a
jackal, and an otter. And the four of them sat in the evenings and spoke
of what was good.

2 And the hare said to his friends, Know ye the day of observance? For
it is a day to give; and to him that gives on that day, a great fruit
shall come. Let us give, then, of what we have, to any who comes asking;
and in the morning, if one comes, let us give it. And they agreed; and
the four lay down in their places, and slept, and were light of heart.

3 And in the early hour the otter went to the river, and found seven red
fish that a fisherman had left on the sand, and he took them, and put
them in a hollow. And the jackal found in a hut a lizard, and a pot of
curds, and a skewer of meat, and brought them. And the monkey took
mangoes from the tree, ripe, and set them by. And each said, I have
something to give.

4 But the hare thought, I eat only grass; and grass is not a thing to
give a guest; and I have nothing else. And he thought for a long time,
and he thought, If one comes to me, I will give my own body. And this
was thought, in the wood, in the hour before the day, and heard by
Sakka, who is the king of the gods, and whose throne grew hot with it.

5 And Sakka took the form of a Brahmin, and came, and stood before the
four, and said, I am hungry; I have come a long way. And the otter said,
Here are seven fish; and the jackal, Here is meat and curd; and the
monkey, Here are mangoes; and the Brahmin said, I will return after the
three have laid them out, and I will see what the fourth has; and he
turned to the hare.

6 And the hare said, Brahmin, I have nothing but grass, and that is not
a gift; but I will give myself. Light a fire, and when it is ready I
will go into it, and thou shalt eat when it is cooked. And Sakka by his
power made a fire, and it burned; and the hare, before he went, shook
himself three times, lest there be a creature in his fur that should die
in the flames, and then leapt, in perfect gladness, and the fire did not
burn him, and was cool, as snow upon a leaf.

7 And Sakka revealed himself, and said, Wise one, thy virtue shall be
known to the end of this age; and he squeezed the mountain, and with the
juice of it he drew upon the face of the moon the likeness of a hare.
And it is there. And every night, whoever looks up, may see it, and the
hare in the moon is not a story about a hare; it is the hare.

XIV. THE BOOK OF THE BRIDE
(THE PEOPLES OF THE NORTH: THE LAY OF THRYM)

1 Wroth was Vingthor when he awoke, and his hammer he missed; his beard
shook, his hair bristled; the son of Jord groped about him. And first of
all these words he uttered: Hearken now to what I say, Loki; what no man
knows on earth, nor in heaven above: the god's hammer is stolen.

2 And they went to the fair court of Freyja, and Thor said, Wilt thou
lend me thy feather-dress, that I may find my hammer? And Freyja said, I
would give it thee were it of gold, and I would lend it thee were it of
silver. And Loki flew, and the feather-dress whirred, until he came
beyond the lands of the gods, and into the land of the giants.

3 Thrym sat on a mound, the lord of the giants, plaiting gold collars
for his hounds, and trimming the manes of his horses. And he said, How
fares it with the gods? How fares it with the elves? Why art thou come
alone to Jotunheim? And Loki said, Ill fares it with the gods and ill
with the elves; hast thou hidden the hammer of Hlorrithi? And Thrym
said, I have hidden the hammer eight leagues under the earth; no man
shall get it again, unless he bring me Freyja to wife.

4 And Loki flew back, and the feather-dress whirred, and he told Thor
the word of Thrym. And they went to Freyja, and said, Bind on thee,
Freyja, the bridal linen; we two shall drive to Jotunheim. And Freyja
was wroth, and snorted with anger; all the halls of the gods trembled;
the great necklace of the Brisings started from her. And she said, Most
lustful of women should I be called if I drove with you to Jotunheim.

5 Then Heimdall spoke, wisest of the gods, for he knew the future like
the Vanir: Let us clothe Thor with the bridal linen; let him wear the
great necklace of the Brisings. Let keys jingle by his side, and woman's
dress fall about his knees, and on his breast let us lay jewels, and set
a neat cap upon his head. And Thor said, The gods will call me womanish
if I let myself be clothed in bridal linen. And Loki said, Be silent,
Thor, such words are of no use; the giants will soon dwell in Asgard if
thou dost not fetch thy hammer.

6 So they clothed Thor in the bridal linen, and with the great necklace,
and Loki went with him as the maid, and they drove the goats home, and
the mountains burst and the earth burned with fire. And Thrym said,
Stand up, giants, and strew the benches; they bring me Freyja, the
daughter of Njord, to wife. And the bride sat down, and ate an ox, and
eight salmon, and all the dainties that were meant for the women; and
drank three casks of mead.

7 And Thrym said, Who ever saw a bride bite more sharply? I never saw a
bride eat more, nor a maid drink more mead. And the maid, who was Loki,
sat by, and answered the giant's word: Freyja has eaten nothing for
eight nights, so eager was she for Jotunheim. And Thrym lifted the veil,
and desired to kiss her, but started back the length of the hall: Why
are Freyja's eyes so terrible? Fire seems to burn from them. And the
maid said, She has not slept for eight nights, so eager was she for
Jotunheim.

8 Then they brought the hammer in to hallow the bride; they laid
Mjollnir in the maiden's lap; and then Thor laughed in his heart, who
was hard of mood, when he felt the hammer in his hand. He slew Thrym the
king of the giants, and crushed all the race of the giants. And so Thor
got his hammer back. And this is the manner in which the god of thunder
was a bride, and it is told as it was, and is not told otherwise.

XV. THE BOOK OF THE HEAD
(THE PEOPLES OF THE SEA: THE THEOGONY AND THE HYMNS)

1 In the beginning of the third age, Cronus, who had taken the throne of
heaven from his father with a sickle of adamant, was told that a child
of his own would take it from him. And he devoured his children as they
were born: Hestia, and Demeter, and Hera, and Hades, and Poseidon; and
he swallowed them whole, and they lived within him, and were not
digested, for they were gods.

2 And Rhea, his wife, being with child with Zeus, went to Crete, and
bore him in a cave; and she wrapped a stone in swaddling clothes, and
gave it to Cronus, and he swallowed the stone, and thought it a child.
And Zeus was nursed by a goat, and fed by bees, and guarded by the
Curetes, who beat their shields that the god should not hear the infant
cry. And in due time he returned, and gave Cronus a drink, and Cronus
brought up the stone, and his five children after it, whole, and grown.

3 And Zeus, being king, took to wife Metis, whose name is counsel, who
was the wisest of the gods and of mortal men. And Gaia and Ouranos said
unto Zeus that Metis would bear a daughter of equal strength to himself,
and after her a son who would be the lord of gods and men. And Zeus,
forestalling this, deceived Metis with soft words, and swallowed her;
and he was pregnant.

4 And the days of the carrying were completed; and Zeus suffered a pain
in his head so grievous that the heavens rang with it, and the sea
answered with a great wave, and the gods looked upon him; and there was
no remedy. And Zeus cried aloud, and sent for Hephaestus, who is the
smith, and said, Take thy axe, and cleave my head.

5 And Hephaestus took the double axe, and struck, and the head of Zeus
was opened; and out of it leapt Athena, fully grown, in her armour of
bronze, and her spear in her hand, with a war cry that shook the whole
of Olympus, and the earth, and the waters. And the sun stopped in its
course, for the wonder of it; and Helios stood his horses, until the
goddess had put by her shield.

6 And Zeus was relieved of the pain, and looked upon his daughter, and
was glad; and he has never been known to repent of what he did to her
mother, though Metis is said to be still within him, and to give him
counsel, from his belly, in a small, wise voice; and it is the counsel
that makes him the wisest of the gods, though it comes from the one he
swallowed.

7 And Athena was given the city that was named for her; and the olive;
and the owl; and the weaving of wool; and the care of those who think;
and she has never needed a mother, for she had a father who was a head.
And the compilers have set the account down in the order in which the
Greeks set it, and in the voice in which they told it, and it is not for
the compilers to say that any part of it is out of order.

XVI. THE BOOK OF THE RED BEER
(THE PEOPLE OF THE TWO LANDS: THE BOOK OF THE HEAVENLY COW)

1 It came to pass in the reign of Ra, when Ra was king of the gods and
of men, that his majesty began to grow old; his bones were of silver,
his flesh of gold, and his hair of lapis lazuli. And mankind, perceiving
that the king was old, spoke against him in their hearts, and plotted,
in the places where they were not heard; and Ra heard them.

2 And Ra said to his followers, Summon to me my Eye, and Shu, and
Tefnut, and Geb, and Nut, and the fathers and mothers who were with me
when I was in the Waters; and the gods came, and bowed before him, and
Ra said, Tell me what ye counsel concerning men, who have plotted
against me; for I will not slay them until I have heard your word. And
they said, Send forth thine Eye, that it may smite them.

3 And the Eye of Ra went down, as the goddess Hathor, and smote mankind
in the desert; and she was well pleased with the slaughter; and she
became Sekhmet, the powerful one, the lady of the red linen; and she
waded in their blood upon the mountains, and her heart was glad; and the
nights were long, and she was not tired.

4 And Ra said, I have the power to stop her, and I will; I would save
the rest of them, for I am yet their king. And he spoke to his
messengers: Run quickly, to Elephantine, and bring me red ochre, much of
it. And the ochre was brought, and ground by the priestesses of
Heliopolis; and the brewers brewed beer, seven thousand jars of it; and
the red ochre was mixed in, and it was the colour of blood.

5 And in the night, before the dawn of the day when the goddess was to
come to the place, the beer was carried to the fields, and poured out,
and it covered the fields of three palms in depth; and Ra said, It is
good; thus will I save mankind. And at the dawn the goddess came, and
looked upon the fields, and saw them flooded with what seemed to her
blood; and her face was reflected there, and was beautiful, and she was
pleased.

6 And she stooped, and drank; and it was good, and she drank more; and
her heart was glad within her, and she became drunk, and she did not
perceive mankind. And she went back to Ra, and Ra said, Come in peace, O
Hathor, for the lady is returned. And she was Hathor again, the lady of
love, and of joy; and the slaughter was not completed, and men lived.

7 And it was decreed that at every festival of the goddess, in the Year,
jars of red beer should be brewed in the same number, and the
priestesses should drink, and the whole of the land should drink with
them, and should dance and sing; and it is so done; and it is the oldest
feast on the earth; and it is the feast of a mercy that was brewed.

XVII. THE BOOK OF THE CAVE
(THE PEOPLE OF THE ISLANDS OF THE SUN: THE KOJIKI)

1 Now Amaterasu, the goddess of the sun, who rules the Plain of High
Heaven, sat in her sacred weaving hall, weaving the garments of the
gods; and her brother Susanoo, the storm, who had been sent from the
heavens for his rages and had returned to say farewell, was not content
with leaving. And he broke down the ridges between her rice fields, and
filled in her irrigation ditches, and fouled the hall in which she
tasted the first fruits.

2 And when the goddess did not rebuke him, but said that he must have
been drunk, and meant well, he grew worse; and he flayed a piebald colt
of heaven, backward, and cast it through a hole broken in the roof of
the weaving hall, and a weaving maiden, seeing it, was so startled that
she struck herself upon the shuttle, and died. And Amaterasu was afraid,
and went into the Heavenly Rock Cave, and shut the door with a stone.

3 And the Plain of High Heaven was dark, and the Central Land of Reed
Plains was dark; and perpetual night came; and the voices of the myriad
evil deities were as the buzzing of summer flies, and all calamities
arose. And the eight hundred myriad gods assembled in the dry bed of the
Heavenly River, and took counsel how to entice her out; and Omoikane,
the god of thought, who thinks for many, had a plan.

4 And they gathered the long-singing birds of eternal night, and made
them sing; and they took the iron from the Heavenly Mountain and made a
mirror; and of the curved jewels they made a necklace; and they uprooted
a sacred tree and hung the mirror upon its middle branches and the
jewels upon its upper; and they hung offerings of blue and white cloth
from the lower; and the god of the offerings held them forth, and
Ame-no-Koyane recited a prayer.

5 And Ame-no-Uzume, the goddess of dawn and of laughter, turned a tub
bottom up before the door of the Rock Cave, and stood upon it; and she
stamped, and made a great noise; and she danced as one possessed, with
clubmoss for a sash and a bundle of bamboo grass in her hand; and the
eight hundred myriad gods laughed together, and the Plain of High Heaven
shook with the sound.

6 And Amaterasu in the cave was astonished, and she opened the door a
very little, and said, Since I have hidden, the Plain of High Heaven
must be dark, and the Reed Plains also; why then does Uzume dance, and
why do the gods all laugh? And Uzume said, We rejoice and dance, because
there is here a deity more illustrious than thou. And at this the mirror
was held up, and the goddess looked, and saw a shining face, and thought
it a stranger's, and came a step nearer to see it.

7 And the god of the strong hand, who stood hidden beside the door, took
her by the hand and drew her out; and another god stretched a rope of
straw behind her, saying, Thou mayest not go back farther than this. And
the Plain of High Heaven and the Reed Plains were light again, of
themselves; and the sun rose, and rises; and the rope is still hung at
the shrines of the country, as a promise that she may not go in again,
and it is the oldest of the ropes.

XVIII. THE BOOK OF THE BUTTERFLY
(THE PEOPLE OF THE WAY: THE BOOK OF CHUANG TZU)

1 Once Chuang Chou dreamed he was a butterfly, a butterfly flitting and
fluttering about, happy with himself and doing as he pleased. He did not
know that he was Chuang Chou. And he was happy, and there was nowhere he
had to be; and the flowers were many, and he went to each of them in
turn, and did not ask which was the better.

2 Suddenly he woke up, and there he was, solid and unmistakable Chuang
Chou. And he sat upon his bed, in his room, and he was the man who had
woken, and was very much a man, with a name, and a back that ached, and
a beard to be combed; and he did not know whether it was Chou who had
dreamed he was a butterfly, or a butterfly who was dreaming he was Chou.

3 And he considered the matter for a long time; and a disciple came and
asked what he considered; and Chuang Chou told him; and the disciple
said, Master, it is surely a plain question: thou art a man. And Chuang
Chou said, And if the butterfly asks the same question, is he not right
to say that he is a butterfly? And the disciple said nothing, and went
away, and fetched tea.

4 And Chuang Chou said that between Chou and the butterfly there must be
some distinction; for there was the one, who was awake, and the other,
who was not; and that this is called the transformation of things. And
he said no more about it, for he was a man who knew when a thing had
been said; and the disciple wrote it down, and it is as the disciple
wrote it.

5 And it is told that when his wife died, Chuang Chou sat with his legs
spread out on the ground, beating on a tub and singing; and his friend
Hui Tzu came to mourn, and said, Thou hast lived with her, and she
brought up thy children, and grew old; not to weep is enough; but to
beat a tub and sing, is that not too much? And Chuang Chou said, It is
not so. When she first died, how could I not grieve? But I looked back
to her beginning, before she was born, and she had not yet a form, nor a
breath, nor a life.

6 And between the confusion of nothingness something changed, and there
was a breath; and the breath changed, and there was a form; and the form
changed, and there was life; and now there is another change, and there
is death. It is like the progress of the four seasons, spring, summer,
autumn, winter. And she is lying peacefully in the great room; and for
me to go about weeping would show that I did not understand fate; so I
stopped.

7 And in the evening the butterfly came to the window, in the lamplight,
and was a butterfly, and went again, into the dark, and did not return;
and Chuang Chou watched it go, and did not follow, and did not say that
it was or was not himself; and went in to his supper, a man, with a
beard, and slept; and it is not recorded what he dreamed.

XIX. THE BOOK OF THE JAWBONE
(THE PEOPLE OF THE GREAT OCEAN: THE TALES OF MAUI)

1 In the beginning the days of the world were short. The sun rose early
and was soon gone again, and the people had no time to do their work.
And the mother of Maui, whose name was Taranga, hung her cloth out to
dry upon the stones in the morning, and before it had dried the night
was come. And she wept, and it was seen by her youngest son, who was
Maui, who was clever, and was not tall.

2 And Maui said, Mother, I will see to it. And he went to his brothers,
and said, We will catch the sun, and we will make him go slowly. And the
brothers laughed, for the sun is a god, and a fire, and could not be
caught; and Maui said, I have a plan. And they plaited ropes of flax,
and they plaited them with the hair of Maui's sister Hina, whose hair
was strong, and they twisted them tight with their hands, and the ropes
were the thickest that had been made in the world.

3 And they travelled many nights, by the dark of the earth, toward the
place where the sun rises; and the way is long, and they lay up through
the days, that the sun should not see them go; and they came to the
east, to the great pit from which the sun climbs; and there they made a
long wall of clay, and wove a net, and set the snares in a row, where
the sun would put his head.

4 And at the dawn, Tama-nui-te-ra the sun, climbed up out of the pit;
and first came his head, and the loops caught him about the head, and
the ropes drew taut; and he roared, and he beat the heavens with his
light, and the ropes held; and the brothers hauled upon them, until
their hands bled, and the sun was held in the snare, and could not rise,
and the day stood still.

5 And Maui stood out before the sun, and took in his hand the jawbone of
his grandmother Muri-ranga-whenua, which he had carried with him all the
way, the same jawbone with which he had once fished up the islands out
of the sea; and he struck the sun with it; and struck him, many times,
with all his might, until the sun was weak and cried out, Why dost thou
treat me thus? Dost thou not know that I am a god?

6 And Maui said, I know that thou art a god; and I will let thee go, if
thou wilt promise to go more slowly across the sky. And the sun was in
pain, and was lame, from the blows of the jawbone, and he gave his word;
and the ropes were loosed; and from that day the sun has moved slowly,
being lame, and the days are long enough for the drying of a cloth, and
for the work of the people, and for their rest.

7 And that is why the sun limps across the sky; and why, at the rising,
the light is red, as with the marks of a blow; and why, in the long days
of the summer, when he goes slowest, the people say, This is the sun
that Maui beat, and was forgiven, and has kept his word. And it is not
to be said that he does it unwillingly, for he was a god, and a promise
is a promise.

PART THREE: WHAT ALL THE ACCOUNTS AGREE ON

XX. THE PART EVERYONE AGREES ON

1 And in the end, past all of it, past the six days and the eight days,
past the ark and the ladder and the wheel, past the argument about the
calendar and the argument about the word for the one who keeps the book,
every account says the same small thing, in its own alphabet, near the
back, where no one looks.

2 Be good to the stranger. For thou wast a stranger in the land of
Egypt; and he who was a stranger is at thy door; and the door is thine
to open, and it is the only door in the matter, and it is not locked.

3 Feed whoever is hungry. Feed him before thou asketh his name, and
before thou knowest his people; for hunger has no creed, and bread has
none, and the one who is fed will tell thee his name, in his own time,
with his mouth full.

4 Do not be cruel because it is cheap. Cruelty is the cheapest of the
things; it costs a moment, and is paid for by a lifetime, and not by the
one who spends it; and the ledger, wherever it is kept, has an entry for
it, and the entry is in the same hand as all the others.

5 Forgive faster than is comfortable. It is not that the wrong was
small; it was not; it is that the one who carries it carries it alone,
and that the carrying is the heavier part; and the one who sets it down
is lighter, and does not become a fool, but only lighter.

6 That is the whole of it. The rest is commentary; and the commentary is
nine hundred pages; and the commentary is where all the trouble comes
from; and it is not to be thrown away, for it was written by people who
loved the text, and who were trying to keep it from being forgotten; and
it may be read, and it may be left; but it is not the text.

7 Go now. Wash thy hands. Eat what is set before thee. Say a word to the
one who is next to thee. It is later than thou thinkest, and it is
earlier than thou fearest; and there is time, and there is bread, and
there is the door; and thou art not alone in the house.

$FG,14$$TX+CX,"THE CHARTER"$$FG$
$HL$
The specification was a size. 100,000 lines, and not one
more, for the whole operating system: kernel, compiler,
editor, graphics, games and documentation together.

A modern kernel alone is around thirty million.

$FG,11$Type $FG,14$LINES$FG,11$ in the terminal to audit this one
against the same budget.$FG$

$TR,"THE PANEL"$
$FG,11$MUS$FG$ and $FG,11$SFX$FG$ are pots. Drag them round, scroll, or
use the arrow keys. Ten detents each. Both start at 0.

$FG,11$VHLD$FG$ and $FG,11$HHLD$FG$ are the hold controls. They start
locked at 5. Take one off centre and the picture goes
with it, exactly like the set your grandmother hit.

$FG,11$LOBBY$FG$ is the music switch. It keeps playing over the
desktop, not just the splash.

The clicks the panel makes are not routed through SFX.
Plastic does not have a volume knob.

$FG,14$NOTES ON THE MACHINE$FG$
$HL$
640x480. 16 colours. One voice.
No network. No ads. No permission asked of anyone.

The compiler is the shell.
The shell is the editor.
The editor is the OS.

$FG,11$Press SOURCE and type over this. It saves itself.$FG$

$SP,"ark"$ $FG,14$AN OFFERING OF 640 KILOBYTES$FG$
$HL$
It is enough. It was always enough.
The rest was decoration.

$MA,"RING THE BELL",LM="BellRing(7);"$
$MA,"RUN THE LOOP",LM="I64 i; for(i=0;i<7;i++) \"%d\\n\", i;"$

$FG,14$$TX+CX,"RING 0"$$FG$
$HL$
There is one ring and everything runs in it. No user mode,
no process isolation, no permission checks, no system call
boundary to cross. Any code can touch any byte.

That is not an oversight. It is the whole design: a single
address space is why the compiler can be the shell and why
a document can be a program.

$FG,12$It also means there is nothing to catch a fault.$FG$
A bad pointer does not raise an exception for somebody
else to handle. It drops you into the debugger, where you
were always going to end up anyway.
